body: Is `logoutUrl.data.logout_url` an internal URL or an external URL? If the latter (based on "the downstream service", it seems that way), using `history` directly or even `location.href = ...` might be more appropriate.

It's a 3rd party system which we host and is behind the same domain.

Our workaround is to use `window.location`, but in reality it would be good to not have to refresh the window. It essentially triggers a cookie to be deleted and the user is redirected to the login screen

My use-case is slightly different, but boils down to a similar option to disable prefetch for `router.replace`.

I'm using `router.replace` to replace only the query string of the current page with some new state (in my case pagination information). Currently this causes a HEAD request that is always unnecessary because the query string is only consumed client side.

I'm using `router.replace` over manually calling `history.replaceState` because the latter does not keep `router.query` in sync.
We are working on some related updates that will fix this issue.

> @dan-j Unless I'm missing something, I think there is a side issue with this. The `HEAD` request has to happen always from client as it is what allows it to determine wether it can do a client side navigation or it must ask the server what's gonna happen next.
> 
> Imagine the case where there is an authentication middleware that checks on a cookie. Once the client loads the page, if you click on a page _protected_ by the Middleware, we must check against it if navigation is going to be successful or if it is going to be blocked. When it is successful we'd simply navigate from client while if it's not we'd do a hard navigation which can lead to a redirect. A similar case happens on _rewrites_ when you have a `Link` to `/foo` but from Middleware you rewrite to `/bar`. In that case the client must pre-fetch and navigate to `/bar` but to get to know it it must "ask" the middleware which is why it needs to run a `HEAD` request.
> 
> My point with this is that it is not just about pre-fetching.. opting out can still cause issues. What we can consider to provide for these use cases is disabling client navigation for pages affected by Middleware but this might turn into a pretty bad user experience because we'd be potentially disabling client-side navigation for the whole app if you have a root middleware. I think disabling `prefetch` on `Router.push()` will not really help your use case. Considering all this, am I correct?

Apologies for the delayed response. Missed the notification and have just been prompted back to it by the latest comment.

I can't remember the exact problem and why `window.location` wasn't desirable, and I'm no longer in active involvement with that project. However, I think I understand your point.

What do you mean by your last comment? Does this mean an option is going to be added, or there's another underlying issue related to @queicherius's comment which will be fixed?

I'm by no means an expert in Next so take this paragraph with a pinch of salt (I raised this issue after helping one of our other front-end devs, so I'm also coming at it with 2nd-hand information), however it sounds like an option to disable pre-fetching still wouldn't be the worse thing to add, but with documentation along the lines of "your mileage will vary". There could be use cases where users know what their URL represents (similar to what @queicherius has mentioned) and don't care for Next trying to do the right thing.

issue.title: Fix shallow routing with rewrites/middleware
issue.body:
Shallow route changes did not work for rewritten pages when Middleware
was used, and made hard refreshes, although it was possible with static rewrites.

This happened because the router has a manifest of the static rewrites,
allowing static rewrites to map the route before comparing with the
local cache.

Middleware rewrites are dynamic and happening on the server, so we
can't send a manifest easily. This means that we need to propagate
the rewrites from the data requests into the components cache in
the router to make sure we have cache hits and don't miss.

This commit does exactly that and adds a test to verify that it works.

This fixes #37072 and fixes #31680

_Note:_ there's one thing that is somewhat an issue though: if the first
page the user lands on is a rewritten page, and will try to make a
shallow navigation to the same page--we will make a `fetch` request.
This is because we don't have any client cache of the `rewrite` we just
had.

## Bug

- [x] Related issues linked using `fixes #number`
- [x] Integration tests added
- [ ] Errors have helpful link attached, see `contributing.md`
